analysis.investment_thesis: Ashapura is a cyclical industrial minerals play in recovery mode — EBITDA grew from INR 167 Cr (2021) to INR 469 Cr (2025) and ROE is a solid 27%, but the 9-year revenue CAGR of just 4.9% and persistently negative free cash flow make this a muddy story, not a ten-bagger. At P/E 15.5 the valuation isn't punishing, but debt is growing faster than the business and I can't get excited about a commodity miner I can't "invest in what I know."
key_strengths: Strong ROE of 27.1% and EBITDA momentum — growing from INR 194 Cr (2022) to INR 469 Cr (2025), a near 3x recovery.
Diversified industrial minerals portfolio (bauxite, bentonite, kaolin, proppants) serving multiple end-markets reduces single-product concentration risk.
P/E of 15.5 is undemanding for a company in cyclical recovery, and FII holding at 19.25% signals credible institutional interest.
key_risks: Persistently negative FCF — worsening from -INR 2 Cr (2022) to -INR 208 Cr (2025) as capex (INR 401 Cr in 2025) outstrips operating cash generation.
Finance costs growing at 17.8% CAGR vs. revenue CAGR of 4.9% — debt servicing is eating the business; D/E at 0.86 exceeds my 0.6 comfort level.
Extremely volatile earnings history — net profit swung from +INR 162 Cr (2016) to -INR 327 Cr (2019) to +INR 383 Cr (2020, inflated by INR 487 Cr other income) — this is a cyclical, not a compounder.
red_flags: Revenue of INR 2,739 Cr in 2025 barely exceeds INR 1,775 Cr in 2016 — 9 years of 4.9% CAGR is a slow grower masquerading as a recovery story.
Net profit is plateauing: INR 282 Cr (2024) vs. INR 289 Cr (2025) — growth stalling just as heavy capex peaks at INR 401 Cr, a dangerous combination.
The INR 383 Cr 2020 net profit was largely fictitious for quality purposes — driven by INR 487 Cr 'other income,' masking core earnings weakness.
analysis.detailed_analysis: As Peter Lynch, I classify Ashapura as a **cyclical with turnaround characteristics** — precisely the type that looks compelling after a recovery but demands discipline. The EBITDA recovery from -INR 17 Cr (2020) to INR 469 Cr (2025) is genuinely impressive, and the operating margin at 11.4% is acceptable for a minerals business. ROE of 27% is real and encouraging. But the 9-year story tells a different truth: revenue in 2016 was INR 1,775 Cr; nine years later it's INR 2,739 Cr. That's not a fast grower — that's a company that collapsed and crawled back. The PEG at ~15.5 P/E against a 9-year earnings CAGR of 6.6% gives a PEG of ~2.3 — far above my 1.0 threshold. Even using recent 3-year net profit growth, the story is noisy because of the massive 2020 other-income spike.\n\nWhat kills my enthusiasm is the capital allocation picture. Free cash flow has been negative every year — deteriorating to -INR 208 Cr in 2025 — while capex accelerated to INR 401 Cr. Borrowings have risen from INR 441 Cr (2020) to INR 1,228 Cr (2025), and finance costs are compounding at 17.8% annually, nearly 4x the revenue growth rate. The CWIP collapsed from INR 504 Cr to INR 72 Cr between 2024 and 2025, meaning this capex cycle just completed — if the new capacity drives a revenue step-change to INR 4,000+ Cr and turns FCF positive, the thesis improves materially. But I need to *see* that, not hope for it. For now, this is a HOLD for believers in the Indian minerals export cycle — not a BUY for new money.
